lead: No two measurements of the same quantity agree exactly, and a control network has more measurements than the unknowns it fixes. Adjustment chooses the one set of values that fits all the observations best, giving more say to the better ones. The better ones are those with larger weights, and the rule that fixes the best values is least squares: the sum of the weighted squares of the residuals is made a minimum. Few syllabi list this topic by name, but every triangle closure and traverse adjustment in a control survey uses it.
prereq: You need: triangle closure and traverse misclosure from Triangulation and trilateration and Horizontal and vertical control.

blocks.text: Errors are of three kinds. Mistakes (a misread vernier, a wrong station sighted) are removed by checks and repeated observations, never by adjustment. Systematic errors follow a law and keep their sign (a tape that is too long, collimation error, curvature); they are removed by corrections or by the method of observing. Accidental (random) errors are what remains: small, equally likely positive or negative, and they are what adjustment deals with.

The true error of an observation is its value minus the true value, which is never known. The most probable value is the best estimate of the true value from the observations, and a residual v is an observation minus the most probable value. The standard error σ measures the spread of an observation; the probable error is 0.6745σ, the error that half the observations exceed.
The weight w of an observation is a number proportional to its trustworthiness, w ∝ 1 ÷ σ². Only ratios of weights matter. The laws of weights used in surveying follow from it:

items: The mean of n equally good observations has n times the weight of one, and standard error σ ÷ √n.
An angle measured n times (repetitions or sets) has weight n.
A levelled height difference over a run of K km has weight 1 ÷ K, because its variance grows in proportion to the length; the same holds for a taped line.
If a quantity is multiplied by a constant c, its weight is divided by c²; the weight of a sum or difference of two quantities is 1 ÷ (1/w₁ + 1/w₂).

blocks.text: The most probable values are those that make Σwv² a minimum. For repeated measurements of one quantity, setting the derivative of Σw(l − x)² to zero gives the weighted mean. With more unknowns, each observation is written as an observation equation in the unknowns; minimising Σwv² gives one normal equation per unknown, and the normal equations are solved together.

Weighted mean:  x = Σwl ÷ Σw
Standard error of unit weight:  σ₀ = √[Σwv² ÷ (n − u)];   of the mean:  σ<sub>x</sub> = σ₀ ÷ √Σw
blocks.where: l are the observations, w their weights, v = l − x the residuals, n the number of observations and u the number of unknowns (1 for a single quantity, so n − u = n − 1). σ₀ is the standard error of an observation of weight 1.

blocks.text: To form a normal equation for an unknown, multiply each observation equation by its weight and by the coefficient of that unknown in it, and add. For a levelling net with two unknown RLs x and y fixed from a benchmark of RL 100.000 m by the equal-weight observations x − 100.000 = 2.512, y − x = 1.836 and y − 100.000 = 4.352, the normal equations are 2x − y = 100.676 and −x + 2y = 106.188, giving x = 102.513 m and y = 104.351 m; the loop's 4 mm misclosure is shared as 1.3 mm on each line.

Two simple results are used constantly. In a triangle whose angles have weights w₁, w₂, w₃, the closing error is distributed in proportion to 1 ÷ w (inversely as the weights), with the opposite sign; with equal weights it is shared equally. At a station where angles are measured and their sum is also measured, the discrepancy is shared in the same way.

After adjustment, look at each residual. Under random errors about 68 % of residuals lie within ±σ and nearly all within ±3σ, so a residual larger than about 3σ points to a mistake: that observation is checked or repeated, not simply adjusted. A value of σ₀ far above what the instruments should give also says that something systematic was missed.

examples.question: The angles of a triangle are measured with different numbers of repetitions, giving weights: A = 48°18′32″ (weight 1), B = 63°27′46″ (weight 2) and C = 68°14′04″ (weight 3). Find the most probable values of the angles.
steps: Sum = 48°18′32″ + 63°27′46″ + 68°14′04″ = 180°00′22″, so the error is +22″ (spherical excess negligible).
Corrections are in proportion to 1 ÷ w: 1, 1/2 and 1/3. Their sum is 11/6.
The weakest angle (A, weight 1) takes the largest share, as it should.

examples.question: The difference of level between two benchmarks is found by three levelling runs: 12.436 m over 2 km, 12.448 m over 3 km and 12.440 m over 5 km. Find the most probable difference, the residuals, the standard error of a 1 km run and the standard error of the result.
steps: Residuals v = l − x: −4.6 mm, +7.4 mm, −0.6 mm.
σ₀ = √(28.9 ÷ (3 − 1)) = √14.5 = 3.8 mm, the standard error of a 1 km run.
σ<sub>x</sub> = 3.8 ÷ √1.0333 = 3.7 mm. The largest residual, 7.4 mm on a 3 km run, is under 3σ for that run (3 × 3.8 × √3 = 19.7 mm), so no run is rejected.
examples.answer: Most probable difference 12.441 m (12.4406 m); residuals −4.6, +7.4 and −0.6 mm; σ for a 1 km run 3.8 mm; standard error of the result 3.7 mm.

traps: Weighting a levelling run in proportion to its length. A longer run is less reliable, so w ∝ 1 ÷ K.
Weight from σ instead of σ². Halving the standard error makes the weight four times, not twice.
Distributing a triangle error in proportion to the weights. It goes in proportion to 1 ÷ w; the best angle gets the smallest correction.
Dividing Σwv² by n. The divisor is n − u, the number of redundant observations.
Adjusting a mistake. A residual of several σ means a blunder to be found and remeasured, not shared out.

quiz.q: Define weight, residual and most probable value.
quiz.a: Weight: a number proportional to the reliability of an observation, w ∝ 1 ÷ σ². Residual: an observation minus the most probable value. Most probable value: the value that makes the sum of weighted squared residuals a minimum.

quiz.q: Why does a 5 km levelling run carry one-fifth the weight of a 1 km run?
quiz.a: Random errors add from set-up to set-up, so the variance of a run grows in proportion to its length. Five times the length gives five times the variance and so one-fifth the weight.

quiz.q: Observations 10.2, 10.3 and 10.1 m have weights 3, 2 and 1. Find the weighted mean.
An angle has σ = 6″ for one measurement. What are the standard error and the weight of the mean of 9 measurements?
quiz.a: σ = 6 ÷ √9 = 2″; weight 9 relative to one measurement.

quiz.q: In the levelling example, a fourth run of 12.475 m over 2 km is added. Should it be used?
quiz.a: Its residual from 12.441 m is +34 mm. For a 2 km run σ = 3.8 × √2 = 5.4 mm, so the residual is over 6σ: almost certainly a mistake (a misread metre or a disturbed change point). It is rejected and the run repeated, not averaged in.

quiz.q: A student adjusts every triangle of a net separately by sharing its closing error equally. Is that a full least-squares adjustment? Explain.
quiz.a: No. It satisfies each triangle's angle condition but ignores the conditions that tie triangles together (side and bearing conditions through the net), so a station reached by two routes can still get two positions. A full adjustment forms all conditions or observation equations together and solves the normal equations once, giving one consistent set.

beyond: Not for the exam. Network adjustment software forms observation equations for every angle, distance and GNSS baseline, weights them from their standard errors, solves thousands of normal equations at once, and reports error ellipses for each station. Statistical tests on the residuals find blunders automatically. Search for least squares network adjustment, error ellipse and blunder detection.
